name: The Apostolic Fathers and Their Writings

objectives.text: Identify the Apostolic Fathers as church leaders who lived soon after the apostles, some of whom learned directly from them
Name Clement, Ignatius, and Polycarp as early church leaders who wrote letters to churches
Retell how early church leaders wrote letters to teach and encourage churches, as the apostle Paul had done
Explain that Christ kept building his church after the last apostles died, using Jesus' promise in Matthew
Summarize the account of Polycarp's faithful testimony before the Roman official as told in the Martyrdom of Polycarp
Describe who Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch, and Polycarp of Smyrna were and the city where each served
Distinguish the inspired writings of the apostles from the helpful but uninspired writings of the Apostolic Fathers

List the main writings in the Apostolic Fathers collection, including 1 Clement, the letters of Ignatius, Polycarp's Letter to the Philippians, the Didache, the Epistle of Barnabas, and the Shepherd of Hermas
Explain the purpose of 1 Clement as a letter urging the Corinthian church to end its division and restore its elders
Analyze the Didache's instructions on baptism, the Lord's Supper, prayer, and fasting as evidence of early Christian worship
Compare Ignatius's teaching on bishops, elders, and deacons with the New Testament pattern of church office
Explain how the Apostolic Fathers' quotations of New Testament books show which writings the early church already received as Scripture
Explain how Ignatius's letters affirm that Christ truly took on flesh, suffered, and rose from the dead
Construct a timeline placing the Apostolic Fathers and their writings in relation to the apostles and key events of the late first and early second centuries
Interpret passages from the Apostolic Fathers using their historical setting, audience, and purpose
Evaluate Clement's teaching on justification in 1 Clement 32 to 33 against Paul's teaching and the Reformed confession of justification by faith alone
Assess why some early churches read writings such as the Shepherd of Hermas publicly while the church did not receive them into the canon
Evaluate how the Reformed tradition uses the Apostolic Fathers as historical witnesses while holding them under the authority of Scripture
Construct an argument from primary sources for the continuity of the church's teaching from the apostles through the Apostolic Fathers

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies: identifying the Fathers, Polycarp, letters to churches, church continuing after the apostles, Polycarp's martyrdom account, Clement and Ignatius, Scripture versus the Fathers, the Didache, Ignatius on church office, New Testament preservation, the timeline, Clement on justification, and historical continuity. Dropped the 'apply standing firm' objective because it aimed at personal response. Dropped the vague oral-to-written transition. Dropped the apologetic arguments against paganism, which belong to the Apologists sibling. Added objectives on the contents of the collection, the purpose of 1 Clement, Ignatius's teaching on Christ's true flesh, reading primary sources in context, why Hermas was not received as canon, and the Reformed use of the Fathers under Scripture. Replaced loose references with verse-specific passages and with Westminster Confession articles that state each doctrine.
